blocks.text: The newborn examination is one of the highest-yield pediatric OSCE stations because it tests whether you can assess a neonate systematically, recognize normal transitional findings, identify congenital abnormalities, and detect signs of infection, respiratory distress, cardiac disease, neurological problems and birth trauma.

The key difference from an older-child examination is that you must be gentle, keep the baby warm, minimize unnecessary handling, and use the baby's natural state—quiet, awake, feeding, crying or asleep—to your advantage.
“You are asked to perform a complete newborn examination on this baby and present your findings.”

items: “Examine this baby following a difficult delivery.”
“Examine this baby for signs of neonatal sepsis.”

subsections.subsection_title: What you are trying to achieve

blocks.text: A complete newborn examination should answer:

G — General appearance V — Vital signs A — Anthropometry S — Skin H — Head F — Face/eyes/ears/nose/mouth C — Chest & cardiovascular A — Abdomen G — Genitalia H — Hips/limbs N — Neurological examination
“Good morning. My name is Dr ____. I have been asked to perform a complete examination of your baby.”
“I will examine the baby from head to toe, including the heart, lungs, abdomen, hips and neurological system.”
“The examination should not be painful. I will keep the baby warm and minimize unnecessary handling.”
This is particularly important in neonates.
This is an important OSCE mark.
Look at the baby from the end of the cot.
A healthy term neonate should generally appear:

items: “The baby has a strong, vigorous cry appropriate for age.”

blocks.text: “The baby's cry is weak and relatively high-pitched, which is abnormal and would warrant assessment in the clinical context.”
Normal newborn temperature is generally around:
Persistent hypothermia or fever is significant.
Count for a full minute because neonatal breathing can be irregular.
G — Grunting R — Retractions U — Use of accessory muscles N — Nasal flaring T — Tachypnea

“The baby is tachypneic at 72 breaths per minute with nasal flaring, intercostal and subcostal recession, and audible expiratory grunting. There is increased work of breathing consistent with neonatal respiratory distress.”
Acrocyanosis can occur transiently in healthy newborns, particularly shortly after birth.
Plot appropriately on a neonatal/infant growth chart.
Maternal diabetes is an important cause.
Measure around the largest occipitofrontal circumference.

items: “The head circumference is appropriate for gestational age.”

blocks.text: “The head circumference is below the expected range for gestational age, suggesting microcephaly.”
Do not rely on visual assessment alone to determine bilirubin severity.
If jaundice is clinically suspected, bilirubin should be assessed according to the relevant neonatal protocol.

content_groups.group_title: Q: When is neonatal jaundice concerning?

blocks.text: Very early onset, rapidly increasing jaundice, severe jaundice, prolonged jaundice, jaundice with illness, or jaundice involving the palms/soles.
Jaundice within the first 24 hours of life is pathological until proven otherwise.
“There is mild jaundice involving the face and upper chest. The baby is otherwise clinically well, with no pallor, hepatosplenomegaly or neurological abnormalities.”

“There is marked generalized jaundice extending to the palms and soles. The baby is lethargic with poor feeding. This is concerning for significant neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and requires urgent bilirubin assessment and evaluation for complications.”
White, creamy material on the skin.
Fine hair, particularly in premature babies.
Blue-grey patches, commonly over the sacral area.
A persistently tense/bulging fontanelle may suggest:
“The anterior fontanelle is tense and bulging while the infant is calm, which is abnormal and raises concern for raised intracranial pressure.”
Don't interpret a fontanelle while the baby is vigorously crying without context.
“The anterior fontanelle is noticeably depressed, with associated dry mucous membranes and reduced urine output, suggesting dehydration.”
Some degree of molding and overlapping sutures can be normal immediately after vaginal delivery.

items: May become more apparent after birth

blocks.text: “There is diffuse soft scalp edema over the presenting part that crosses suture lines, consistent with caput succedaneum.”
“There is a localized fluctuant swelling over the right parietal region that does not cross the suture lines, consistent with a cephalohematoma.”
“There is diffuse boggy scalp swelling with increasing head circumference and associated pallor and tachycardia. This is concerning for a subgaleal hemorrhage and requires urgent assessment.”
One side of the face may move less during crying.
“There is asymmetry of the lower face during crying, with reduced movement on the left side, suggesting possible facial nerve dysfunction.”
Symmetrical red reflex in both eyes.
“The red reflex is absent from the right eye, raising concern for an opacity along the visual axis such as congenital cataract and requiring ophthalmological assessment.”
Low-set ears can be associated with:
Chromosomal or syndromic abnormalities, although the finding is nonspecific.
In a newborn with respiratory distress, ensure the nasal passages are patent.
Bilateral choanal atresia is an airway emergency.
Inspect the roof of the mouth.
If required, gently palpate the palate with a gloved finger.
“There is a visible cleft involving the hard and soft palate.”
Remember to consider feeding and aspiration implications.
“There is marked micrognathia with posterior displacement of the tongue and associated respiratory/feeding difficulty.”
“The baby has reduced spontaneous movement of the right upper limb with tenderness over the clavicle, raising concern for a right clavicular fracture.”
A newborn's chest may have transient breast enlargement.

items: Respiratory distress syndrome depending on context
Reduced air entry on one side

blocks.text: “There is marked respiratory distress with reduced air entry over the right hemithorax and asymmetry of chest expansion, raising concern for a right-sided pneumothorax.”
Always palpate femoral pulses in a newborn.
Weak or absent femoral pulses may suggest:
“The femoral pulses are significantly weaker than the brachial pulses bilaterally, with delayed femoral upstroke. This raises concern for aortic coarctation.”
Not every neonatal murmur means congenital heart disease.
“There is a grade 2/6 systolic murmur best heard at the left upper sternal border, without a palpable thrill.”

“The baby has central cyanosis involving the tongue and oral mucosa, with oxygen saturation below the expected range. This is concerning for significant cardiopulmonary disease and requires urgent assessment.”
A newborn abdomen should generally be:
“There is periumbilical erythema with purulent discharge and surrounding skin inflammation, concerning for omphalitis.”
A small liver edge may be palpable in a newborn.
Interpret findings according to degree and clinical context.
“The liver edge is palpable approximately 3 cm below the right costal margin and is smooth and non-tender.”
Then interpret according to the baby's age and clinical context.
“The spleen is palpable below the left costal margin and is firm and non-tender.”
Newborn kidneys can sometimes be more readily palpable than in older children.
Meatus is located on the ventral surface rather than at the tip.
“The urethral meatus is located on the ventral aspect of the penis rather than at the glans tip, consistent with hypospadias.”
Palpate both scrotal sacs and inguinal canals.
“The right testis is palpable within the scrotum, while the left testis is not palpable within the scrotum or along the inguinal canal.”
Don't immediately call every non-palpable testis an intra-abdominal testis—you haven't established its location.
Mild labial swelling can be normal.
A small amount of vaginal discharge or bleeding can also occur because of maternal hormonal influence.
Look for absence or abnormal position of the anus.
“The normal anal opening is not visible in the expected position, raising concern for an anorectal malformation.”
Screen for developmental dysplasia of the hip.
Assesses whether a hip can be displaced from the acetabulum.
Assesses whether a dislocated hip can be reduced.
Do not repeatedly force or perform rough hip movements.
A palpable "clunk" as the femoral head reduces into the acetabulum.
“There is a palpable clunk on the left Ortolani maneuver, suggesting reducible hip instability.”
Avoid calling a subtle "click" a positive Ortolani.
A palpable displacement/instability of the femoral head with gentle provocation.
“The right hip demonstrates instability on Barlow testing, with a palpable shift suggesting a dislocatable hip.”
C — Cavus A — Adduction V — Varus E — Equinus
“The right foot is held in a cavus, adducted, inverted and plantar-flexed position, consistent with talipes equinovarus.”
“There is a midline lumbosacral cystic swelling covered by a thin membrane, concerning for a neural tube defect such as myelomeningocele.”
A simple shallow sacral dimple can be benign.
A healthy term newborn generally has:
Floppy, with reduced resistance to passive movement.
“The infant demonstrates generalized hypotonia with reduced spontaneous flexion and poor resistance to passive movement.”
Hold the baby's head and shoulders safely.
Allow a controlled slight head extension/startle stimulus.
“The Moro reflex is present but asymmetrical, with reduced movement of the right upper limb, raising concern for peripheral nerve or musculoskeletal injury.”
Turn toward the stimulus and open the mouth.
Place a clean gloved finger appropriately.
Place your finger in the baby's palm.
Stimulate the sole near the toes.
An asymmetric reflex can be more clinically significant than a reflex that is simply difficult to elicit.
Here is a model presentation you can actually use:

“This is a term neonate who appears well, alert and comfortable at rest, with a strong cry and spontaneous symmetrical movements. The baby is pink and well perfused with no central cyanosis, pallor or significant jaundice. Respiratory rate and heart rate are within the expected neonatal range, with no respiratory distress. Anthropometric measurements are appropriate for gestational age.

The head is normally shaped with normal sutures and a soft, non-bulging anterior fontanelle. The eyes are symmetrical with normal red reflexes bilaterally. The ears, nose and mouth are normally formed, with an intact palate. There are no obvious dysmorphic features.

The chest is symmetrical with good bilateral air entry and no added sounds. Cardiovascular examination reveals normal heart sounds, good peripheral pulses including palpable femoral pulses, and no significant murmur.
The abdomen is soft and non-distended, with no palpable masses or significant organomegaly. The umbilicus appears healthy. The genitalia and anus are normally formed.

The spine is normal with no obvious neural tube defect. The limbs are symmetrical with normal digits and no obvious deformity. The hips are stable on screening examination. Neurologically, the baby has normal tone, symmetrical movements and appropriate primitive reflexes.

items: Overall, this is an unremarkable newborn examination.”

blocks.text: This is the section to practice repeatedly.

“The baby appears lethargic and less responsive than expected, with a weak cry and reduced spontaneous movement. The temperature is abnormal, and there is tachypnea with increased work of breathing. Peripheral perfusion is reduced with delayed capillary refill. These findings are concerning for significant neonatal illness, including possible neonatal sepsis.”
Findings → interpretation, rather than immediately declaring sepsis.

“The preterm infant is tachypneic with nasal flaring, intercostal and subcostal recession and expiratory grunting. Air entry is reduced bilaterally but relatively symmetrical. The findings are consistent with significant neonatal respiratory distress, and in this preterm infant respiratory distress syndrome would be an important consideration.”

“The baby is lethargic with poor spontaneous movement, reduced tone and a weak cry. Suck is poor and the primitive reflexes are reduced. These findings indicate significant neurological depression and, given the perinatal history, would raise concern for hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy.”

“There is marked generalized jaundice extending to the palms and soles. The baby is lethargic and feeding poorly. This is concerning for significant neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, and urgent bilirubin measurement and assessment for bilirubin encephalopathy would be required.”
“The baby has visible jaundice within the first day of life. Given the early onset, this should be regarded as pathological until investigated.”

“The baby has central cyanosis involving the tongue and oral mucosa. There is increased work of breathing and oxygen saturation is below the expected range. Femoral pulses are palpable. These findings indicate significant cardiopulmonary disease, and cyanotic congenital heart disease would need to be considered.”

“The upper limb pulses are stronger than the femoral pulses, with delayed femoral upstroke. There is a systolic murmur over the precordium. The pulse findings are concerning for coarctation of the aorta.”

“There is a continuous murmur best heard over the left upper sternal border, with otherwise good peripheral pulses. In the appropriate clinical context, this may represent a patent ductus arteriosus.”
Remember that the murmur and clinical findings depend on the timing after birth and physiology.
“There is a harsh pansystolic murmur best heard at the lower left sternal border, without central cyanosis. In the appropriate clinical context, this could represent a ventricular septal defect.”

“There is a visible cleft involving the upper lip extending toward the nostril, with an associated palatal defect. This represents a cleft lip and palate and has implications for feeding, airway management and further multidisciplinary care.”
“The urethral opening is located on the ventral aspect of the penis rather than at the tip of the glans, consistent with hypospadias. The testes are both palpable within the scrotum.”

“The right testis is palpable within the scrotum. The left hemiscrotum is empty and the left testis is not palpable along the inguinal canal. This is consistent with a non-scrotal left testis, requiring appropriate follow-up.”
“The left foot is fixed in plantar flexion, inversion and adduction with associated cavus, giving the appearance of talipes equinovarus.”

“There is instability of the right hip on Barlow testing and a palpable clunk on Ortolani testing. This is concerning for developmental dysplasia of the right hip and requires appropriate imaging/follow-up.”

“The baby has reduced spontaneous movement of the left arm and appears uncomfortable when the limb is moved. There is localized swelling and tenderness over the left clavicle. These findings are suggestive of a clavicular fracture.”

“The right upper limb is held close to the body with the elbow extended and forearm pronated, with reduced spontaneous movement. The Moro reflex is asymmetric. This pattern raises concern for an upper brachial plexus injury.”
This classic posture is often described as:
“There is erythema and swelling around the umbilicus with purulent discharge. The baby also appears lethargic. These findings are concerning for omphalitis with possible systemic infection.”

“There is diffuse, fluctuant scalp swelling extending across suture lines, with increasing head circumference and associated pallor and tachycardia. This is highly concerning for subgaleal hemorrhage, which is a neonatal emergency.”
“There is a localized, well-defined scalp swelling over the right parietal bone that does not cross the suture lines, consistent with a cephalohematoma.”
“There is diffuse, soft scalp edema over the presenting part that crosses suture lines, consistent with caput succedaneum.”
“There is a midline lumbosacral cystic swelling associated with an abnormal overlying skin appearance. This is concerning for a neural tube defect, such as myelomeningocele.”
Do not press on the lesion.
“The baby has reduced spontaneous flexion, poor resistance to passive movement and reduced primitive reflexes, indicating generalized hypotonia.”
Then discuss possible causes based on history.
A baby with poor feeding should be assessed broadly.
“The baby has a weak suck and poor feeding, associated with lethargy and reduced spontaneous activity. These findings are concerning for systemic neonatal illness and require further assessment.”

content_groups.group_title: Q1. What are the normal heart and respiratory rates in a newborn?

blocks.text: Heart rate is generally around 100–160 bpm, while respiratory rate is approximately 30–60 breaths/minute.

content_groups.group_title: Q2. Why must you keep the newborn warm?

blocks.text: Neonates have limited thermoregulatory capacity and can lose heat rapidly, leading to hypothermia and increased metabolic stress.

content_groups.group_title: Q3. What does central cyanosis mean?

blocks.text: Cyanosis involving the tongue and oral mucosa indicates significant arterial desaturation and requires urgent assessment.

content_groups.group_title: Q4. What is the significance of absent femoral pulses?

blocks.text: It raises suspicion for coarctation of the aorta.

content_groups.group_title: Q5. What is the difference between caput and cephalohematoma?
Q6. Which is more dangerous: cephalohematoma or subgaleal hemorrhage?

blocks.text: Subgaleal hemorrhage, because substantial blood loss can occur into the subgaleal space, leading to hypovolemic shock.

content_groups.group_title: Q8. What primitive reflexes should you assess?

blocks.text: You should know that additional neonatal reflexes may also be assessed depending on the examination.

content_groups.group_title: Q9. What does an asymmetric Moro reflex suggest?

blocks.text: Peripheral nerve injury, particularly brachial plexus injury, or musculoskeletal injury such as clavicular fracture.

content_groups.group_title: Q10. What does a bulging fontanelle suggest?

blocks.text: Possible raised intracranial pressure, including meningitis or intracranial hemorrhage, depending on the clinical context.

content_groups.group_title: Q11. What does a sunken fontanelle suggest?

blocks.text: Dehydration, particularly when associated with other clinical signs.

content_groups.group_title: Q12. When is neonatal jaundice particularly concerning?

blocks.text: Jaundice within the first 24 hours, rapidly progressive/severe jaundice, jaundice associated with illness or neurological abnormalities, and prolonged jaundice.

content_groups.group_title: Q13. What are the causes of neonatal respiratory distress?

blocks.text: RDS, TTN, meconium aspiration, pneumonia/sepsis, pneumothorax, congenital heart disease and congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

content_groups.group_title: Q14. What are the important causes of central cyanosis?

blocks.text: Respiratory disease, cyanotic congenital heart disease, persistent pulmonary hypertension and severe systemic illness, among others.
❌ Leaving the baby exposed and cold.
❌ Starting with vigorous examination instead of observing first.
❌ Forgetting to count respiratory rate for a full minute.
❌ Not examining the clavicles after a difficult delivery.
❌ Not examining the spine and sacrum.
❌ Describing an abnormality without interpreting its significance.

subsections.subsection_title: HOW TO REPORT TO THE EXAMINER

blocks.text: Don't give a long unstructured list.

content_groups.group_title: GENERAL → POSITIVE FINDINGS → IMPORTANT NEGATIVES → INTERPRETATION

blocks.text: “This is a term neonate who appears mildly unwell. The baby is tachypneic at 70 breaths per minute with nasal flaring, subcostal recession and expiratory grunting. There is central cyanosis and oxygen saturation is reduced. Femoral pulses are palpable and there is no obvious abdominal mass. These findings indicate significant neonatal respiratory/cardiorespiratory compromise, and urgent assessment is required.”
This sounds much more clinically competent than:
Suppose the baby has jaundice and hypotonia:

“This is a neonate who appears lethargic with reduced spontaneous activity and a weak cry. There is marked jaundice extending to the palms and soles. The baby has reduced tone and a poor suck. These findings are concerning for significant neonatal hyperbilirubinemia with possible neurological involvement, and urgent assessment is required.”
Suppose the baby has a cardiac problem:

“This is a neonate with central cyanosis and increased work of breathing. The heart rate is elevated and oxygen saturation is reduced. There is a systolic murmur over the precordium, although femoral pulses are palpable. The findings are concerning for significant cardiopulmonary disease, including congenital heart disease, and require urgent evaluation.”
Suppose you find multiple congenital abnormalities:

“The baby has several dysmorphic features including low-set ears, a broad nasal bridge and generalized hypotonia. There is also a cardiac murmur and bilateral single transverse palmar creases. These findings raise concern for an underlying syndromic condition, and I would recommend a full dysmorphology assessment and appropriate cardiac and genetic evaluation.”
Notice that you don't diagnose a syndrome solely from a few physical findings unless the station specifically gives enough information.
